extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media organizations, policymakers, researchers, and the informed public
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the dimensions by which Americans judge the news media — trust, perceived bias, informational role, and effects on democracy — based on a large national survey. Useful for those assessing media institutions or designing interventions to restore public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the news media to democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans still value the media’s traditional roles in society; 81% say the news media is “critical” (42%) or “very important” (39%) to democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a baseline evaluative metric: how essential citizens believe the media is to a healthy democracy. Related measures include prioritization among media roles (accuracy, informing the public, holding power accountable). The report notes that despite valuing these roles, many say the media performs poorly at them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing accurate and fair news reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Large majorities (88%) say it is “critical” or “very important” for the news media to provide accurate and fair news reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a core quality criterion for news organizations. The executive summary contrasts the high importance placed on accuracy with public evaluations that media is not adequately meeting this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring Americans are informed about public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighty-eight percent say it is critical/very important for the news media to ensure Americans are informed about public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of media’s informational function. The report connects deficits here to worries about being well-informed given the modern information environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding leaders and powerful interests accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighty-two percent of Americans say it is important for the media to hold leaders accountable for their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates investigative and watchdog responsibilities of journalism. Public perception of failure in this role contributes to negative assessments of media performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived political bias in news coverage (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: A majority see political bias in news coverage: 46% see 'a great deal' and 37% a 'fair amount' of political bias overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dimension measures perceived systemic bias across the media environment, a primary driver of distrust and polarization in media evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived bias in respondents’ primary news source
rubrics_metrics.description: Most Americans see bias in the news source they rely on most; 21% see 'a great deal' and 36% a 'fair amount' of bias in their go-to source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates personalization of bias perceptions — not just general skepticism but distrust directed at specific outlets people use most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern about bias in others’ news vs own news
rubrics_metrics.description: More Americans are concerned about bias in the news other people are getting (64%) than say they worry about their own news being biased (34%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures third‑person or partisan perceptions: people tend to see bias as a problem for others more than for themselves, which affects polarization and debates over media reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception that reporting inaccuracies are intentional
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans perceive inaccurate news to be intentional: 52% say reporters are misrepresenting the facts and 28% say reporters are making facts up entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between viewing errors as accidental versus purposeful manipulation; high levels of perceived intentionality correlate with deep distrust and views that media are trying to persuade rather than inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief about distrusted media’s intent (persuade vs incapable of accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly 3 in 4 Americans (74%) say news organizations they distrust are trying to persuade people to adopt a certain viewpoint, while 16% say those outlets are trying to report accurately and fairly but are unable to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether distrust is attributed to malicious intent versus incompetence; stronger attribution to persuasion implies more adversarial public attitudes toward those outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan differences as primary predictor of media opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Political party is the primary determining factor: two-thirds of Republicans (67%) have 'very' or 'somewhat' unfavorable opinions of the news media versus 20% of Democrats and 48% of independents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that party affiliation strongly conditions evaluations across every aspect of media performance; any assessment of media trust should disaggregate by party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generational/age differences in media attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Views also vary by age: older Americans are generally more favorable toward the news media than younger Americans (43% favorable age 65+ vs 20% favorable under 30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age is an important demographic covariate; the report links some age differences to generational news consumption patterns (e.g., online news consumers being less attached to local communities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of reporting staffs (hiring to increase diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong majority (75%) say news organizations should hire to increase the diversity of their reporting staffs, though this ranks lowest among media priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public supports newsroom diversity, but priorities for what diversity should focus on differ sharply by politics and race (e.g., Democrats and Blacks emphasize racial/ethnic diversity; Republicans and Whites emphasize diversity of political views).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misinformation online as a major problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Three in 4 Americans (74%) say the spread of misinformation online is 'a major problem,' exceeding other media-environment challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames misinformation as the top media-related threat; complements public desire (70%) for major internet companies to find ways to exclude false/hateful information online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling overwhelmed by volume/speed of news and coping responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Americans feel overwhelmed by volume and speed: 60% say it is harder to be well-informed because of all the sources, and responses to feeling overwhelmed include relying on one or two trusted sources (39%), consulting a variety of sources (30%), tuning out entirely (18%), or relying on others to sort facts (9%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures perceived information overload and behavioral adaptations; useful for evaluating how media supply-side changes affect public information habits and civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief about whether there are enough sources to sort facts vs too much bias to sort facts
rubrics_metrics.description: More Americans (51%) say there are enough media sources to sort out the facts than say there is so much bias it's difficult to sort out the facts (45%), a slight improvement from 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures public assessment of the informational marketplace’s capacity to self-correct versus being irreparably biased; partisan splits are large (Republicans more likely to say too much bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of local news in political and civic engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Local news plays a key role: 33% follow local community issues 'very closely' (up from 25% in 2017). Those who follow local news closely are more likely to vote in local elections, feel attached to their communities, and less likely to feel powerless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates the civic benefits of local journalism and links local news consumption with higher civic engagement and community attachment; notes that primarily online news consumers (often younger) are less knowledgeable about local affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception that the media bears blame for political division and potential to heal
rubrics_metrics.description: Forty-seven percent say the media bears 'a great deal' of blame for political division while 49% say the media could do 'a great deal' to heal those divisions (34% say a 'moderate amount').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses normative judgments about media’s social impact — both culpability in fostering division and responsibility/opportunity to reduce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptions of political attacks on the media and their justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventy-seven percent say the media is under attack politically, but opinions divide: 66% of Democrats say the attacks are not justified while 58% of Republicans say the attacks are justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures whether public sees political criticism of media as legitimate or as an unfair threat — an indicator of polarization in media legitimacy.
